units.title: Operator dispatch, trace correlation and fusion groups
outcomes: Trace one framework operator from dispatcher through backend to executed kernels and name each boundary.
Capture correlated PyTorch-profiler and NVTX timelines and attribute one host gap before reading kernel counters.
Identify one fusion group and state which launches and materializations it removes.
units.why: A faster kernel changes nothing when the framework dispatches a different path. The trace shows which path ran and where time actually went.

next.note: Turn dispatch gaps into launch-overhead and graph-capture decisions.
Use the traced path as the insertion point for a custom operator.

study.title: Exact profiler and range call contracts
study.locator: Overview example with `activities`, `schedule` and `on_trace_ready`; API reference for `torch.profiler.profile` parameters `activities`, `record_shapes` and `with_stack`, `torch.profiler.record_function` and `export_chrome_trace`

study.title: Whole-graph versus regional compile boundary
study.locator: `TinyTransformerBlock` and `BaselineRegionalCompileBenchmark` in `baseline_regional_compile.py` versus `RegionalMLP` and `compile_mlp` in `optimized_regional_compile.py`; run with `python -m ch13.compare`

focus: Follow one `aten` operator to its CUDA API call and kernel in both the profiler table and the `nsys` timeline. Name the dispatcher, backend, launch and kernel boundaries.
Label each phase with `torch.profiler.record_function` and `torch.cuda.nvtx.range`. A CPU range ending does not prove its GPU work finished.
Compare the whole-block and MLP-only compile pair: regional compile keeps dynamic-shape regions eager to avoid recompilation while fusing the compute-heavy subgraph.
units.reproduce: Without notes, profile a 1024 by 1024 `torch.float32` CUDA matrix multiply wrapped in `torch.profiler.record_function("mm")` and `torch.cuda.nvtx.range("mm")`. Capture a short `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=none --cpuctxsw=none` trace, follow one `aten::mm` entry to its kernel, and reconcile profiler CUDA time with the union of kernel intervals and completed wall time.
traps: Reading profiler CUDA time as kernel latency when CUPTI is unavailable. The table then falls back to legacy timing without a device trace.
Treating `record_shapes=True` or `with_stack=True` as free. Both add overhead and hold tensor references during capture.
Calling a fused graph faster without checking which materialization it removed. Count launches and intermediates before and after.

selfTest.q: Does the end of an NVTX range prove the kernel it launched has finished?
selfTest.a: No. The range ends when host code ends. GPU completion needs event synchronization or trace correlation.

selfTest.q: Two kernels each run 5 ms fully overlapped. What device busy time do they establish?
selfTest.a: 5 ms, the union of their intervals. Summing them to 10 ms double-counts overlap.

selfTest.q: Why does the regional-compile pair keep attention and LayerNorm eager?
selfTest.a: Those regions carry dynamic shapes and masks that would trigger recompilation. Fusing only the MLP keeps the gain without the recompile cost.

selfTest.q: Profiler shows one `aten::add` but the timeline shows no kernel. What is the most likely cause?
selfTest.a: A shape or guard miss ran a fallback path, or the profiler grouped the op while the kernel ran on a stream the trace filter excluded. Check dispatch and capture boundaries before blaming the kernel.

units.title: Launch overhead, CUDA graphs, bucketing and graph misses
outcomes: Measure per-launch overhead with interleaved event trials and report medians, not best runs.
Capture and replay a stable kernel sequence in a CUDA graph with static buffers and an eager fallback.
Name one bucketing or graph-miss regime where graphs lose and show the measured crossover.
units.why: Small decode steps are often launch-bound, not kernel-bound. Graphs remove the host overhead only for stable shapes with a tested fallback.

next.note: See which request shapes make launch overhead dominate the endpoint.
Attribute a graph win or miss to request-level TTFT and TPOT.

study.title: Capture, replay and graph best practice
study.locator: Chapter 13, Reducing Kernel Launch Overhead with CUDA Graphs: Capturing a CUDA Graph and Preallocating Memory; Replaying the Graph; Best Practices for CUDA Graphs

study.title: Eager launches versus graph replay
study.locator: `BaselineCudaGraphsBenchmark` in `baseline_cuda_graphs.py` versus `OptimizedCudaGraphsBenchmark` in `optimized_cuda_graphs.py` (`N = 1024`, 32000 iterations); diagnostic in `graph_replay_benchmark.py`

study.title: Piece graphs and shape bucketing
study.locator: `BaselinePieceGraphsBenchmark` in `baseline_piece_graphs.py` versus `OptimizedPieceGraphsBenchmark` in `optimized_piece_graphs.py` with `RegionalPieceGraph` in `piece_graphs_model.py`

focus: Name the timed boundary before comparing: per-launch overhead, captured replay, or end-to-end step. Keep warmup, capture and steady-state replay in separate intervals.
Capture on a dedicated nondefault stream with max-size static buffers. Any allocation during capture fails, and any shape change after capture needs a new graph or bucket.
Bucket one graph per stable shape and keep an eager fallback. A replay on an unseen shape silently computes the wrong geometry or fails to launch.
units.reproduce: Time 200 eager launches of a 1024-element vector add against 200 `graph.replay()` calls with CUDA events, interleaved in pairs with a recorded seed, and report both medians. On an RTX 3050 6 GB with CUDA 13.4 a single batch of 200 gave about 8.1 us per eager launch and 5.1 us per replay. Your medians will differ; replay must not exceed eager on this shape, and any shape change needs recapture.
traps: Capturing an allocation or `empty_cache` call inside the capture region. The capture fails or pins a stale allocator state.
Timing capture or warmup inside the steady-state interval and calling that replay latency.
Keeping one graph for all shapes. Unseen geometry replays stale work; bucket explicitly and test the fallback.

selfTest.q: What does graph replay remove from a stable sequence?
selfTest.a: It removes per-launch host overhead and idle gaps between kernels. It does not shorten the kernels themselves.

selfTest.q: Why does a shape change after capture need recapture?
selfTest.a: The replay reuses captured addresses and launch geometry. A new shape needs a new capture or bucket; otherwise the run reads stale buffers or fails.

selfTest.q: Name one regime where CUDA graphs lose.
selfTest.a: When capture, bucket lookup, or replay setup exceeds the saved launch overhead, or when misses force frequent fallback. Small stable batches win; ragged dynamic shapes lose.

units.stopWhen: You report interleaved eager and replay medians with explicit boundaries, a passing fallback test, and one measured losing regime.

fit.note: The book launch-overhead section plus the pinned capture-replay and piece-graph pairs cover overhead, bucketing and misses at measure depth.

units.title: Request lifecycle, continuous batching and the kernel shapes it creates
outcomes: Explain the queue, prefill, decode, sample and completion lifecycle at performance depth.
Predict how continuous batching changes live batch size, kernel shapes and occupancy for a stated arrival mix.
Measure one fair-scheduling effect with heterogeneous request sizes.
units.why: Serving performance comes from the live request mix, not one kernel shape. The lifecycle decides which kernels run at which width every iteration.

next.note: Trace how paged blocks make slot replacement cheap.
Bound prefill-decode interference with chunked scheduling.

study.title: Dynamic, continuous and scheduled batching
study.locator: Chapter 16, Dynamic Batching; Continuous Batching; Continuous Scheduling

study.title: Iteration-level scheduling mechanism
study.locator: Sections 3 to 4, iteration-level scheduling and selective batching with Algorithm 1 and Figures 2 to 5

study.title: Static draining versus dynamic insert
study.locator: `BaselineContinuousBatchingBenchmark` with `dynamic=False` in `baseline_continuous_batching.py` versus `dynamic=True` in `optimized_continuous_batching.py` on `ContinuousBatchingBase`

focus: A request moves through queue, prefill, decode steps, sampling and completion. Continuous batching refills finished slots every iteration instead of waiting for the longest sequence.
Selective batching splits the work: linear and norm layers batch broadly while attention runs per request with its own KV. Kernel shapes therefore track the live mix, not the configured maximum.
Heterogeneous lengths set occupancy and latency: one long prefill can stall short decodes in the same iteration, which fair scheduling and token budgets bound.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, work a four-request mix with decode lengths 10, 10, 10 and 100 under static batching versus continuous batching. Show static batching holds all slots until length 100 while continuous batching frees three slots at length 10, and state which kernel dimensions shrink when the live batch drops from 4 to 1.
traps: Calling any batching continuous because requests share a server. Only per-iteration refill with independent completion counts.
Assuming live batch size equals configured maximum. Finished slots empty the kernels below their configured width.
Reading higher throughput as lower latency for every request. Batching can delay a single request while raising aggregate tokens per second.

selfTest.q: What makes batching continuous rather than static?
selfTest.a: Per-iteration membership: finished requests leave and waiting ones join every token step, without waiting for the longest sequence.

selfTest.q: Why do linear layers and attention see different batch shapes in one iteration?
selfTest.a: They batch across requests while attention needs per-request KV and masks. The batched layers see the live batch width; attention sees per-request sequence state.

selfTest.q: How does one long request hurt short ones in a shared iteration?
selfTest.a: A long prefill occupies the iteration and delays short decodes sharing it. Token budgets and scheduling priorities bound that stall.

practice.name: Companion code ch15: continuous batching pair

practice.note: Single-GPU run is enough. No public autograder scores the schedule; retain the arrival mix, both throughputs and the kernel-shape notes.

units.stopWhen: You can walk one request through every lifecycle stage and show measured throughput and queue-wait differences for static versus continuous draining on one mix.

fit.note: The book describes batching behavior but not the iteration-level mechanism; the Orca paper supplies the scheduling algorithm beside the book and the batching lab.

units.title: Paged KV allocation and prefix reuse at kernel level
outcomes: Derive block-table translation, slot waste and per-token KV bytes for a stated model and block size.
Explain prefix-reuse cache identity, including what the hash covers and why partial blocks miss.
Quantify fragmentation and memory-capacity effects on one engine run.
units.why: KV memory sets how many requests fit and which prefixes skip compute. Block tables and reuse identity decide both.

next.note: Reuse the block accounting for chunked-prefill budgets.
Integrate one paged kernel through the FlashInfer wrapper.

study.title: Blocks, manager and scheduling interaction
study.locator: Sections 4.1 to 4.2, PagedAttention and KV Cache Manager with Figures 5 to 7; Section 4.5, Scheduling and Preemption

study.title: Radix tree reuse and cache-aware scheduling
study.locator: Section 3, Efficient KV Cache Reuse with RadixAttention, with Algorithm 1 and Figure 3

study.title: Allocation, pooling and radix reuse lab
study.locator: `BaselineKVCacheManagementBenchmark` in `baseline_kv_cache_management.py` versus `OptimizedKVCacheManagementBenchmark` in `optimized_kv_cache_management.py`; `RadixTree` and `KVCache` in `radix_attention_example.py`

focus: A logical token position maps through a block table to a physical block. Blocks are fixed-size pages, so a 40-token sequence with block size 16 occupies blocks of 16, 16 and 8 with 8 wasted slots.
Only full blocks enter the reuse cache under a hash of parent hash plus block tokens plus extras such as image hashes. A partial final block never hits.
Sharing is reference-counted with LRU eviction. Freeing appends tail blocks first because they hash more context and are less likely to be reused.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive per-token KV bytes as \(2 \times L \times H_{\text{kv}} \times D \times B\) with \(L\) layers, \(H_{\text{kv}}\) KV heads, \(D\) head dim and \(B\) bytes per value. For \(L = 32\), \(H_{\text{kv}} = 8\), \(D = 128\), FP16, get 131072 bytes (128 KiB) per token. Then place a 40-token sequence in block size 16 and report 3 blocks with 8 wasted slots.
traps: Counting cached bytes as free memory. Shared blocks are live for every referencing request until all release them.
Expecting reuse for a shared prefix shorter than one block. Nothing is cached until a full block completes.
Treating the block hash as the tokens alone. Parent context and extras are part of identity; dropping them causes wrong reuse.

selfTest.q: Why does fixed-size paging beat one contiguous reservation per request?
selfTest.a: It avoids external fragmentation from variable-length reservations. Waste is bounded to one partial block per sequence instead of one oversized reservation.

selfTest.q: Two requests share 10 tokens with block size 16. Why is there no reuse?
selfTest.a: Only full blocks are hashed and cached. The partial tail has no stable identity until it fills.

selfTest.q: What does a vLLM prefix-cache hash cover beyond token IDs?
selfTest.a: Parent hash plus block tokens plus extras such as LoRA IDs, image hashes or cache salts. Same text with a different image or salt hashes differently.

practice.note: Single-GPU run is enough. No public autograder checks reuse; retain block tables, hit rates and the capacity notes.

units.title: Chunked prefill, decode interference and long-context regimes
outcomes: Explain chunked prefill, decode interference and the token-budget rule.
Predict per-iteration latency and KV-transfer cost for a stated chunk size and live batch.
Identify the long-context regime where chunking or disaggregation stops paying.
units.why: Long prompts stall every decode sharing the iteration. Chunking and placement bound that stall without changing the attention bill.

next.note: Price quantized and speculative paths under the same interference.
Carry the token budget into endpoint goodput measurement.

study.title: Chunked scheduling and interference
study.locator: Chapter 16, Stall-Free Scheduling (Chunked Prefill); Chapter 15, Prefill-Decode Interference and Impact on Latency (TTFT) and Throughput (TPOT)

study.title: Stall-free batching mechanism
study.locator: Sections 4.1 to 4.3, chunked-prefills, stall-free batching with Algorithm 3, and token-budget selection; Figure 9, coalescing cost

study.title: Staged versus peer KV handoff
study.locator: `HostStagedPrefillDecodeDisaggBenchmark` in `baseline_prefill_decode_disagg.py` versus `PeerPrefillDecodeDisaggBenchmark` in `optimized_prefill_decode_disagg.py` via `prefill_decode_disagg_common.py`

focus: Chunked prefill splits a long prompt into fixed-size chunks that join decode iterations. Total attention work is unchanged; per-iteration latency is bounded by the token budget.
Stall-free batching never pauses decodes to admit a prefill. The scheduler picks a chunk size that fits the token budget alongside live decodes.
Long-context prefill is compute-bound with large activation memory while decode stays memory-bound. Placement and KV-transfer cost decide whether disaggregation pays.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, chunk a 20000-token prompt into 5000-token chunks alongside 8 live decodes with a stated token budget. Show 4 chunks, state which decodes share each iteration, and explain why total attention work is unchanged while the worst per-iteration latency falls.
traps: Calling chunked prefill cheaper in total FLOPs. It bounds latency per iteration; the attention bill stays the same.
Measuring TTFT on an empty server and promising it under load. Interference appears only with live decodes sharing iterations.
Ignoring KV-handoff cost in a disaggregation win. Transfer and scheduling can exceed the stall saved.

selfTest.q: Does chunking reduce total prefill FLOPs?
selfTest.a: No. The same query-key pairs are scored; they are spread across iterations so one iteration never carries the full prefill.

selfTest.q: What is prefill-decode interference?
selfTest.a: It stalls latency-sensitive decodes behind one long compute-bound prefill, raising time per output token. Chunking bounds that stall.

selfTest.q: When does disaggregation stop paying?
selfTest.a: When transfer plus scheduling overhead exceeds the interference saved, or when the live batch is too small to fill the freed iterations.

practice.note: Single-GPU emulation is enough. No public autograder scores the handoff; retain the length, batch, TTFT, TPOT and transfer notes.

study.locator: Chapter 16, Quantization Approaches for Real-Time Inference: Reducing Precision from FP16 to FP8 and FP4; Weight-Only Quantization (GPTQ, AWQ); Fusing Quantization-Dequantization Steps into the Execution Graph; Chapter 15, Constrained Decoding Performance Implications

study.title: Verification cost model
study.locator: Sections 2 to 3, draft-verify-accept loop, acceptance rule \(\alpha = \min(1, q/p)\), resampling distribution and walltime-versus-operations analysis

study.title: Mask reuse and weight-only quantization labs
study.locator: `GuidedDecodingBenchmark` with `reuse_gpu_mask=False` in `baseline_guided_decoding.py` versus `reuse_gpu_mask=True` in `optimized_guided_decoding.py`; `baseline_awq_gptq_smoothquant.py` versus `optimized_awq_gptq_smoothquant_awq.py`

focus: Quantized dispatch changes scales, granularity and accumulation, not just storage. Per-token scales dequantize as \(K_{\text{float}}[h, s, d] = K_{\text{int8}}[h, s, d] \times k_{\text{scale}}[h, s]\); verify error against task tolerance, not just kernel error.

Speculative verification accepts draft token \(t\) with probability \(\alpha = \min(1, q/p)\), where \(p\) is the draft probability and \(q\) the target probability. Rejection resamples from the normalized positive part of \(q - p\) and stops the batch.
Structured decoding pays for masks and host interaction every step. A GPU-resident reused mask removes the per-step rebuild; measure its cost per schema, not as a constant.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, verify the LeetGPU 87 worked example: draft `[1, 2, 0]` with the given draft and target probabilities and uniform samples `[0.50, 0.70, 0.30, 0.90]`. Accept position 0 (\(\alpha = 0.50/0.60 = 0.83\), \(0.50 < 0.83\)), reject position 1 (\(\alpha = 0.20/0.50 = 0.40\), \(0.70 > 0.40\)), resample token 3 from normalized `[0.667, 0, 0, 0.333]`, and emit `[1, 3, 0, 0]`.
traps: Reading a high acceptance rate as a speedup. Verification adds a full batched forward; low acceptance wastes it.
Comparing quantized and dense paths by kernel time alone. Scale, granularity and accumulation change error; gate by task quality.
Treating structured decoding as free once correct. Mask builds and host round trips scale with schema complexity and batch width.

selfTest.q: What does lossless speculative decoding guarantee?
selfTest.a: It preserves the target distribution up to floating-point limits: accepted drafts follow it and resamples come from the adjusted difference. Greedy equality tests check the implementation, not the proof.

selfTest.q: Why does speculative decoding depend on batch shape?
selfTest.a: They change arithmetic intensity and memory traffic per step. Verification adds a batched forward that pays only when acceptance is high enough at that batch width.

selfTest.q: Where does guided-decoding overhead come from?
selfTest.a: A per-step CPU mask rebuild plus host interaction. Reusing a GPU-resident mask removes the rebuild; complex schemas at small batches still cost double-digit percent.

units.title: Multimodal encoder and decoder co-execution
outcomes: Explain encoder and decoder co-execution and how encoder batches change decode geometry.
State the multimodal prefix-hash rule and one false-sharing failure it prevents.
units.why: Images enter as embedding runs inside a text request. Their encoding and hashing decide both batch geometry and reuse safety.

next.note: Integrate encoder and decoder kernels through one serving interface.
Carry encoder placement into endpoint measurement.

study.title: Multimodal throughput and reuse evidence
study.locator: Section 6.2 with Table 2, throughput on LLaVA-v1.5-7B image and LLaVA-NeXT-34B video models, and reported RadixAttention hit rates

study.title: Multimodal block-hash rule
study.locator: Automatic Prefix Caching, hashing example with multi-modality inputs: placeholder runs, per-block image-hash extras, block size 16 with 41 placeholders

focus: The encoder runs once per image or segment while the decoder steps per token. Co-execution shares the scheduler, KV pool and batch slots, so encoder work changes decode batch geometry.
Image regions become placeholder token runs replaced by embeddings at prefill. Prefix identity must hash the image content, not just the placeholder IDs, or different images falsely share KV.
Read Table 2 as a throughput comparison against the stated Transformers baseline with the reported 52.4 percent video and 74.1 percent image cache-hit rates, not as a universal speedup.
units.reproduce: Without notes, sketch one image-plus-text request through prefill and two decode steps: mark where the image encoder runs, which token range the embeddings replace, and which blocks are hashable for reuse when a second request shares the text but not the image.
traps: Batching images as if they were text tokens. Encoder capacity, placeholder expansion and embedding replacement follow different rules.
Hashing only placeholder IDs. Different images then share KV and corrupt output.
Reading a multimodal throughput table without its baseline, bench and hit rate. All three set the result.

selfTest.q: Where does encoder work sit in the request lifecycle?
selfTest.a: It runs once per image input and feeds embeddings into prefill, while the decoder then steps token by token. Its batch slots and KV-pool share affect live decode geometry.

selfTest.q: Do identical placeholder runs imply reusable KV?
selfTest.a: No. Placeholders are identical token IDs; the block hash must include the image hash so different images map to different KV.

selfTest.q: Does the multimodal throughput table promise a general speedup?
selfTest.a: No. It compares stated model pairs on stated benches with stated hit rates. Different images, batch mixes or baselines change it.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: encoder-batch versus decoder-only timing and a multimodal prefix-hash identity check in your integrated endpoint.
units.stopWhen: You can place encoder work on the lifecycle diagram and defend the prefix-hash rule for a shared-text, different-image pair.

fit.note: The SGLang paper reports multimodal throughput but not input-hash identity; the vLLM prefix-caching design supplies the multimodal block-hash rule beside it.

focus: Caller-owned workspace comes first: allocate the 128 MB float buffer aligned to 16 bytes, call `plan` with `indptr`, `indices` and `last_page_len`, then reuse the plan across layers with `run`. `plan` never runs inside a graph or `torch.compile`.

units.reproduce: Without notes, register the fused residual-add plus RMSNorm as a custom op with a fake shape rule, allocate the FlashInfer decode workspace, `plan` a batch of 7 requests in `NHD` layout with `page_size = 16`, and `run` one layer. State which buffers must stay stable for graph capture and which eager fallback runs on an unsupported dtype.
traps: Calling `plan` inside a captured graph. Planning copies metadata on the host; only `run` with stable bindings captures.
Forgetting workspace alignment or zero-initialization on first use. Split-KV scratch then reads garbage.
Shipping the fast path without a fallback. Unsupported dtypes, layouts orshapes must route to a tested eager path.

selfTest.q: Why does a custom op need a fake implementation?
selfTest.a: Shape inference, compilation and autotuning need output metadata without launching kernels. The fake implementation supplies it; without it capture and compilation fail.

selfTest.q: What is frozen once a graph-safe decode wrapper is planned?
selfTest.a: Batch size, page-table buffers, `q_len_per_req` and workspace binding. A re-plan with different values raises; only order-tensor contents may change without recapture on supported routes.

selfTest.q: Where does a custom kernel sit relative to vLLM, SGLang and FlashInfer?
selfTest.a: vLLM owns scheduling plus paged blocks, SGLang owns radix reuse plus program-level caching, FlashInfer owns the attention and sampling kernels. Your op replaces one kernel behind a stable plan-run boundary, not a scheduler.

practice.name: LeetGPU 83 Fused Residual Add RMS Norm, integrated locally

practice.note: Hosted runs need an account; the reference implementation and tests are public in the challenges repository. Do not stop at the hosted score: the local integration with fallback is the deliverable.

units.stopWhen: Your op passes differential tests through both the custom path and the eager fallback, with a pinned plan-run interface and a stated unsupported-shape policy.

fit.note: FlashInfer supplies the serving-kernel interface, SGLang the alternative architecture, and the companion extension path the local build contract.

units.title: Token, distribution and task-quality equivalence
outcomes: Define token, distribution and task-quality equivalence with predeclared tolerances.
Run a perplexity evaluation with fixed windows, stride and dtype and report the difference.
Gate one optimization on all three equivalence levels.
units.why: Every inference optimization is a correctness claim first. Equivalence at token, distribution and task levels decides whether a speedup ships.

next.note: Use the quality gate as the acceptance check for endpoint changes.
Encode the gate in versioned regression tests.

study.title: Correctness-first debugging gate
study.locator: Chapter 16, Profiling, Debugging, and Tuning Inference Performance: Debugging Correctness Issues

study.title: Perplexity evaluator contract
study.locator: `load_tokens` with space-separated integers; `parse_args` with `tokens`, `--seq-len`, `--stride`, `--dtype` and `--fp8-mode`; `GPTConfig` and `GPTModel` scoring

study.title: Exact-match sampler fast path
study.locator: `GreedySamplerBenchmark` with `materialize_probabilities=True` in `baseline_greedy_sampler.py` versus `False` in `optimized_greedy_sampler.py` via `greedy_sampler_common.py`

focus: Token equivalence is exact ID match under a stated sampling policy. Greedy `argmax` on logits equals `argmax` on probabilities, so the sampler fast path must match exactly.

Distribution equivalence is a measured distance: perplexity difference near noise on a fixed token window plus a KL or logprob check where sampling matters. One perplexity number without windows, stride and dtype is not a gate.
Task equivalence is a product spot-check on a small eval slice. Quantization and speculative paths pass only when all three levels agree within predeclared tolerances.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, prove greedy equivalence on a 50000-token vocabulary with a fixed seed: `argmax` of logits equals `argmax` of `softmax` of the same logits, so skipping probability materialization is exact. Then state the perplexity formula \(\text{PPL} = \exp(\text{mean NLL})\) and which windows, stride and dtype your gate fixes.
traps: Accepting `equal_nan=True` style looseness as correctness. Unexpected NaNs must fail the gate, not pass it quietly.
Widening tolerance until a wrong-mask variant passes. Tolerances are predeclared from precision and use, not fitted to results.
Testing quality on the data the optimization was tuned on. Fix the eval tokens before measuring the difference.

selfTest.q: Does a small perplexity difference alone prove an optimization is safe?
selfTest.a: No. It can hide distribution shifts that sampling exposes and task regressions that perplexity misses. All three levels need tolerances.

selfTest.q: What does the greedy-sampler fast path save, and why is it exact?
selfTest.a: It removes the full-vocabulary softmax and probability buffer from greedy decode. Correctness holds because `argmax` is invariant to monotone softmax.

selfTest.q: What must a perplexity comparison fix?
selfTest.a: Fixed token file, window length, stride, dtype and conversion mode. Changing any of them between runs invalidates the comparison.

practice.name: Companion code ch16: perplexity evaluation gate
practice.locator: Run `perplexity_eval.py` with `tokens`, `--seq-len`, `--stride`, `--dtype` and `--fp8-mode` on a fixed token file before and after one optimization; report perplexity difference with windows and dtype retained
practice.note: CPU or single-GPU run is enough. No public autograder scores the difference; retain the token file, windows, stride, dtype and both perplexities.

units.stopWhen: One optimization carries a written equivalence report with exact-match, perplexity-difference and task spot-check results against predeclared tolerances.

fit.note: The book correctness section plus the perplexity evaluator and the exact-match sampler pair cover token, distribution and task gates.

units.title: Endpoint workloads, request metrics, baselines and attribution
outcomes: Derive KV-capacity and latency floors for a stated model and GPU.
Measure TTFT, TPOT, memory, throughput and goodput on a fixed arrival distribution against strong baselines.
Attribute a kernel change to request-level effect with shares and explain the residual.
units.why: Endpoints are judged by TTFT, TPOT, memory and goodput on a real mix. Attribution connects one kernel change to those numbers without overclaiming.

next.note: Encode the endpoint result and its losing regime in regression gates.
Carry TTFT, TPOT and goodput discipline into serving-system ownership.

study.title: KV, capacity and latency floors
study.locator: kv cache per-token bytes with `k` and `v` across layers, heads and bytes per value; capacity from weights plus KV; latency calculations for memory-bound versus compute-bound floors; batch sizes and flops counting

study.title: Inference profiling and utilization trade-offs
study.locator: Chapter 16, Profiling, Debugging, and Tuning Inference Performance; Profiling with Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute; Maximizing GPU Utilization and Throughput Versus Latency Trade-Offs

study.title: Load test and profiling harness
study.locator: `CompletionRecord`, `run_load_test` with `target_qps`, warmup phase and percentile summaries in `inference_server_load_test.py`; `MonitoringSystem`, `DynamicBatcher` and `PrefixCache` in `inference_profiling.py`

focus: Derive floors before measuring: per-token KV bytes, weight-resident capacity, and memory-bound versus compute-bound latency. A measurement that beats its floor has a boundary error.
Fix the workload first: shape and arrival distribution, TTFT and TPOT SLOs, memory budget and goodput definition. Goodput counts only requests meeting the SLOs.

Attribute with shares: a kernel speedup \(s\) on fraction \(f\) of step time gives at most \(1 / ((1 - f) + f / s)\) end-to-end. Baselines are the production engine and the vendor library, not eager alone.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive capacity for an 8-billion-parameter FP16 model on an 80 GB GPU: weights occupy about 16 GB, leaving roughly 64 GB of the 80 GB budget for KV and workspace. At 131072 bytes per token (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 head dim, FP16), that budget holds roughly 490000 tokens (524288 per 64 GiB); state your GB/GiB convention and workspace reservation. Then show how a 10 percent kernel win on a 30 percent step share gives at most about 3 percent end-to-end.
traps: Quoting a friendly-shape kernel speedup as an endpoint win. Request mix, queueing and uncovered shares dilute it.
Averaging TTFT and TPOT across different lengths and SLOs. Report per-slice percentiles on a fixed distribution.
Keeping only summary speedups. Retain raw samples, workload, revision and machine state or the result cannot be audited.

selfTest.q: What do TTFT and TPOT measure?
selfTest.a: Time to first token (prefill plus scheduling) and time per output token after the first (steady decode cadence). E2E adds queueing and completion.

selfTest.q: Why can throughput rise while goodput falls?
selfTest.a: Throughput counts all tokens; goodput counts only requests meeting latency SLOs. A faster engine with more SLO misses can raise one and lower the other.

selfTest.q: What makes an engine baseline weak?
selfTest.a: It compares against a weak reference instead of the engine and library the team would actually run. The gap overstates the shippable win.

selfTest.q: Does a kernel speedup times its profile share equal the endpoint win?
selfTest.a: No. Divide only after checking the floor: the win must fit inside the helped share, and the residual needs a timeline or counter cause.

practice.name: Companion code ch16: inference load test with baselines
practice.locator: Run `inference_server_load_test.py` with `--duration`, `--target-qps` and `--output-json`; compare one custom path against the production-engine and vendor-library baselines on TTFT p50 and p99, TPOT, memory and goodput with `CompletionRecord` fields retained
practice.note: Keep captures short. Multi-GPU flags exist but single-GPU runs are enough. No public autograder scores the endpoint; retain arrival mix, baselines and raw samples.

units.stopWhen: Your endpoint report shows TTFT, TPOT, memory and goodput on a fixed mix against strong baselines, with the kernel-to-request attribution reconciled to a timeline.

fit.note: The book and load-test harness cover measurement but not analytical floors; the inference-arithmetic reference supplies the KV-capacity and latency bounds beside them.

units.title: Versioned regression gates, fallback and rollback
outcomes: Implement a versioned regression gate with fallback and rollback for one integrated path.
Distinguish a real regression from noise with raw samples and uncertainty.
units.why: An integrated kernel needs a gate that catches regressions and a rollback that restores service. Otherwise the first bad revision ships.

next.note: Operate the gates as part of serving ownership.

study.title: CI gates and production monitoring
study.locator: Chapter 13, Continuous Integration and Performance Benchmarking; Chapter 16, Monitoring System Metrics and Counters

study.title: Versioned expectations harness
study.locator: `expectations_2x_b200.json` and `expectations_b200.json` beside each chapter, refreshed with `--update-expectations`; `BenchmarkConfig` with iterations and warmup in `compare.py`; validity profiles in chapter READMEs

focus: Version every gate: code revision, model and tokenizer identity, config, hardware and toolchain, workload seed and tolerances. A gate without versions cannot roll back.
Gate on correctness and quality first, then on TTFT, TPOT, memory and goodput with uncertainty. A statistically resolved but practically useless gain stays out.
Keep fallback automatic and rollback one command: unsupported shapes route to the eager path, and a failed gate restores the last passing revision with its data.
units.reproduce: Without notes, write the gate contract for your integrated kernel: versioned inputs, correctness plus quality checks, TTFT and TPOT budgets with sample counts, fallback trigger and rollback command. Then seed one wrong-mask defect and show the gate failing before timing is read.
traps: Gating only on mean latency. Tails, memory and quality regress first; gate them with their own budgets.
Updating expectations to match a regression. Expectations change only after validating new hardware or a declared policy change.
Testing rollback without a drill. An untested restore command fails when it is needed.

selfTest.q: What versions does a regression gate pin?
selfTest.a: Code and model versions, config, hardware and toolchain, workload and seed, tolerances and budgets. Without them a rerun is a different experiment.

selfTest.q: Does routing to fallback forgive a regression?
selfTest.a: No. Fallback keeps serving correct while the gate stays red and the rollback restores the last passing revision. Silent fallback without a gate hides the regression.

selfTest.q: When does a timing difference count as a regression?
selfTest.a: Only with raw samples, sample counts and an uncertainty method that respects pairing and drift. A best-run comparison proves nothing.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: `kernellab` versioned regression gate with fallback routing, rollback drill and retained raw samples.
units.stopWhen: A seeded defect trips the gate, fallback serves correctly, and one rollback command restores the last passing revision with evidence retained.

fit.note: The book CI and monitoring sections plus the versioned expectation harness cover gates, fallback and rollback at implement depth.
